Chapter Two: The Hidden World of Tokyo’s Nightlife and the People Who Work There
When the sun goes down, Tokyo reveals a whole new side of itself. The orderly routines of the day slip away, and suddenly you’re surrounded by neon lights, thumping music, and endless possibilities. For a lot of people, it’s the perfect escape—a place to let loose and forget about work or family stress for a while. But if you’re one of the folks working in Tokyo’s nightlife, you quickly learn this world has its own set of rules—and some real risks.
Hostess clubs are a fascinating piece of Japanese culture. They aren’t brothels, but they’re not your average bars either. Most of the customers are men who pay for a little attention—a woman to listen, laugh, and make them feel special for a few hours. Doing this job takes charm, a lot of patience, and honestly, a pretty thick skin. Now, imagine being a foreign woman in that scene. The pay can be great, but it’s easy to feel isolated, standing out in a culture where blending in matters so much. And if you don’t speak Japanese? Even the simplest things can start to feel overwhelming.
Lucie wasn’t alone in Roppongi—far from it. Young women from all corners of the globe came to Tokyo, each with their own reasons: chasing adventure, earning money, maybe just looking for a fresh start. Some of them found the work empowering, almost like they were taking charge of their own stories. Others struggled, worn down by the constant pressure to be “on” and meet everyone’s expectations. The clubs themselves? A lot of them were run by people with their own secrets, and sometimes, the line between what’s legal and what’s not got a little blurry.
The people who came to these clubs were just as varied—lonely businessmen, curious tourists, you name it. Most just wanted some company or a bit of fun. But there were always a few who treated the clubs like hunting grounds. That’s why the women working there became experts at reading people, knowing when to keep their guard up. Still, even the most careful could get caught off guard.
The night Lucie disappeared, she was doing something pretty common for a hostess—meeting a customer outside the club. They called it a “dohan.” The whole point was to build a relationship, to keep those customers coming back. But stepping outside the club’s safety net meant anything could happen.
For the police, the world of hostess clubs was tricky. Sure, the business was legal, but it had a reputation for attracting crime. And if you were a foreign worker? You were often seen as a troublemaker—or worse, your problems just weren’t taken seriously. When Lucie vanished, some officers wondered if she’d just run away, or maybe gotten herself mixed up in something risky. Even when her family insisted she’d never disappear like that, the police were skeptical.
The investigation was slow. Language barriers made it tough to communicate, and cultural differences led to a lot of misunderstandings. The police took their time, careful and methodical, but to Lucie’s family, it just felt like nobody really cared. Leads came and went, but real progress was hard to see. Before long, the media caught wind of the story, and it started to grow—fast.
For the women who’d worked alongside Lucie, her disappearance hit hard. Some became extra cautious; others decided it was time to leave the industry entirely. The sense of safety that drew them to Tokyo in the first place was suddenly gone. The clubs tried to keep things running as usual, but you could feel the shadow of what had happened hanging over everyone.
